title: Who carries the risk?
principle: Take the risk off the buyer, the risk they really fear.

screens.text: Let me take you back to 2010. Flipkart sold books and phones online. But few Indians had a debit or credit card, and many had never paid on a website. What if they paid but the parcel never came? Flipkart had to fix that fear. Guess how.

screens.prompt: Few Indians would pay online first. What do you think Flipkart did?

options.label: Gave big discounts on all orders
Took cash when the parcel came
Ran TV ads with famous film stars

screens.why: It let people pay cash at the door. If no parcel came, the buyer lost nothing. Two months after cash on delivery began, 30 of every 100 sales were paid this way. By 2013, it was 80.

screens.title: Risk reversal
screens.text: Think about who carries the risk. Usually the buyer pays first and hopes, so if it goes wrong, the buyer loses. Flipkart moved that risk onto itself. This is called risk reversal: you carry the risk, so saying yes feels safe for the buyer.

screens.title: Which risk?
screens.text: Here's what many sellers miss. Money is not the only risk. A buyer can also lose time, or feel bad in front of family. Giving money back fixes only the money. So first ask: what is this buyer most afraid of losing?

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Flipkart sold across India, but your home bakery faces the same fear. You've seen this before: in June, "full money back" helped you win the new colony. Now it's August of your fourth year, and a family asks about a ₹6,000 cake for their daughter's engagement.

screens.prompt: The family has never tried your cakes. 150 guests will see this ₹6,000 engagement cake. What worries them most?

options.label: Paying a little more than a shop charges
Serving a bad cake in front of guests
Losing ₹6,000 if they dislike the cake

screens.why: Exactly. ₹6,000 is small next to the whole party. What scares them is a bad cake in front of 150 guests. A refund can't undo that.

wrong.a: A few hundred rupees won't worry a family spending lakhs on a party. What scares them is a bad cake in front of 150 guests.
wrong.c: That's the money risk, and a money-back offer fixes it. But a refund comes after the party. What really scares them is a bad cake in front of 150 guests.

screens.prompt: The family fears serving a bad cake to 150 guests. Which offer would help them feel safe?

options.label: Free tasting, and the cake arrives 3 hours early or it's free
Pay half now, the rest only after the party
Get ₹600 off today, and a free cake next time

screens.why: Yes. The tasting lets them check the cake before the big day. Early delivery leaves time to fix anything, and if you're late, you pay. Now the risk is yours, not theirs.

wrong.b: That moves some money risk onto you, but the fear stays: a bad cake in front of 150 guests. A tasting first and early delivery remove the fear they really have.
wrong.c: A discount and a free cake make the deal cheaper, but the fear stays the same. A tasting first and early delivery remove the real risk.

screens.prompt: 10 families want tasting boxes. Each box costs you ₹300. Then 6 book cakes, and each cake leaves you ₹3,200. What's left?
screens.why: Well done. 6 cakes × ₹3,200 = ₹19,200. All 10 tasting boxes cost ₹3,000, so ₹16,200 is left. Taking the risk has a cost, so always check it against what you earn.

wrong.a: I see what you did: 6 × ₹3,200 = ₹19,200. But the 10 tasting boxes cost you ₹3,000. Take that away, and ₹16,200 is left.
wrong.b: You took away only the 6 boxes for families who booked: ₹1,800. But all 10 boxes cost you, ₹3,000 in all. So ₹19,200 − ₹3,000 = ₹16,200.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six offers. For each one, tell me: does it take a risk off the buyer?
buckets: Yes, it takes a risk off
No, the buyer still carries it

items.text: Pay the last half after the cake arrives
Full payment two weeks before the day
See a photo of the cake 3 hours early, with free fixes
"Best cakes in town!" on your post
A free tasting before a big order

screens.why: Paying later, a photo with time to fix mistakes, and a tasting all move the risk onto you. Paying early and "no changes" leave it with the buyer, and a boast removes no risk at all.

screens.setup: It's late August. The family booked, and you promised: "Delivered 3 hours early, or the cake is free." On the day, heavy rain floods the roads. The cake arrives perfect, but only 1 hour early. The family hasn't noticed. The cake leaves you ₹3,200.
screens.question: What do you do?

options.label: Say nothing. The cake was still on time
options.outcome: You keep the ₹3,200. A week later, the mother checks the time on her phone photos. She tells her sister your promise means nothing. No guest from the party orders from you.
options.why: Your promise only works if people believe it. Breaking it quietly, even once, turns it into empty words.
options.better: Tell them, and keep the promise: the cake is free.

options.label: Tell them, and say the cake is free
options.outcome: You return the ₹6,000. Making the cake cost you ₹2,800, so you lose ₹2,800. The family is amazed and tells everyone. In September, 4 guests order party cakes, leaving you ₹12,800. You end with ₹10,000 more.
options.why: People remember when you keep a promise even though it costs you money. They tell others, and that brings you more orders.

options.label: Explain the rain and give ₹1,000 back
options.outcome: The family thanks you politely. You keep ₹2,200. One guest orders later, leaving you ₹3,200. You end with ₹5,400 more, but now your promise sounds like "free, unless something happens".
options.why: Telling the truth was good. But you changed your promise after the event, and next time buyers may not trust a promise with excuses.
options.better: Keep the promise in full: the cake is free.

screens.text: Find the risk they really ___, and carry it ___.
screens.why: Exactly. Flipkart took on the risk of a parcel that never came. You took on the risk of a bad cake on the big day, and you kept your promise even when it cost you. That's risk reversal.

summary: Risk reversal: you carry the risk, so saying yes feels safe for the buyer.
Find the risk they really fear. Money back can't fix a ruined party, but a tasting first can.
Check what your promise costs you, and keep it even when it costs you money. People remember that.

cards.front: Parents worry their child won't like your tuition class. Which offer helps with that fear?
options: Pay after the first week, only if the child likes it
cards.back: Risk reversal: you carry the risk, so saying yes feels safe.

cards.front: A family fears a bad wedding cake in front of guests. What fixes that fear?
options: A tasting first and early delivery
cards.back: Fix the risk they really fear. A refund after the event can't undo it.

cards.front: You promised "on time or free". You were late, but nobody noticed. What do you do?
options: Tell them, and keep the promise
cards.back: Keep your promise even when it costs you money. People remember that.
